hints: Focus on the structure of the halogenoalkane first, SN1 and SN2 depend strongly on whether the carbon with the Cl is primary or tertiary.
Remember that 1-chloropropane is primary so it cannot form a stable carbocation, while 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is tertiary and forms a very stable carbocation.
For the tertiary halogenoalkane, check the reagent and solvent, ethanolic cyanide gives substitution but ethanolic hydroxide gives elimination to an alkene.
walkthrough:
**Classify the halogenoalkanes**

Think side by side with me. 1-chloropropane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, a primary halogenoalkane. 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCl}$, a tertiary halogenoalkane.

This matters because carbocation stability is tertiary > primary.

**Recall SN1 versus SN2**

SN1 goes in two steps via a carbocation intermediate:
$$\text{R-Cl} \rightarrow \text{R}^+ + \text{Cl}^- \text{ then } \text{R}^+ + \text{Nu}^- \rightarrow \text{R-Nu}$$
It needs a stable carbocation, so only tertiary halogenoalkanes do SN1 readily. Primary halogenoalkanes do SN2 in one concerted step.

**Rule out the primary reactions**

Options A and B both use 1-chloropropane. A primary carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ is too unstable for SN1.

So both are SN2 substitutions, to an amine in A and to an alcohol in B.

**Compare the two tertiary reactions**

Both C and D start from a stable tertiary carbocation $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$, so SN1 substitution is possible. The difference is the reagent in ethanol.

$$\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCl} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCN} + \text{Cl}^-$$
Cyanide acts as a nucleophile to give substitution. Hydroxide in ethanol, however, acts as a base and causes elimination of HCl to form an alkene, methylpropene. That is not SN1.

options.A: Incorrect. 1-chloropropane is primary, so it reacts with ammonia by SN2 to form propylamine and then further amines. It cannot form a stable enough carbocation for SN1.
options.B: Incorrect. 1-chloropropane is primary, so reaction with hydroxide is SN2 substitution to propan-1-ol (if aqueous) or could involve elimination, but it is not SN1 because no stable carbocation can form.
options.C: Correct. 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is tertiary and ionises in the slow step to the stable carbocation $(CH_3)_3C^+$. Cyanide then attacks quickly to give 2-methyl-2-cyanopropane. This two-step nucleophilic substitution via a carbocation is classic SN1.
options.D: Incorrect. Although the substrate is tertiary, potassium hydroxide in ethanol promotes elimination, not substitution. Hydroxide removes a proton to give methylpropene plus water, so this is an elimination reaction, not SN1.
